cards.explanation: The answer is show favoritism, friends. James opens with it: "My brothers, as you hold out your faith in our glorious Lord Jesus Christ, do not show favoritism." (James 2:1) He puts the instruction right alongside holding out their faith in Jesus. Short sentence, big weight.

The answer is a seat of honor, friends. James says the man in fine clothes gets, "Here is a seat of honor…" (James 2:3) The best seat, handed over because of the fine clothes. Meanwhile the poor man hears something very different.

The answer is True, friends. James says the poor man hears, "You must stand…" or "Sit at my feet…" (James 2:3) So he gets standing or the spot at somebody's feet. The man in fine clothes gets the seat of honor, and that's exactly the favoritism James is calling out.

The word is judges, friends. James says they've "…become judges with evil thoughts?" (James 2:4) Nobody handed them a gavel, but sorting people by their clothes is judging all the same. I think that's the sting of it.

The word is poor, friends. James asks, "Has not God chosen the poor of this world to be rich in faith and to inherit the kingdom He promised those who love Him?" (James 2:5) Rich in faith, and an inheritance on top. The ones the seating chart skipped are the ones God chose.

James names the rich, friends. He asks, "Is it not the rich who oppress you and drag you into court?" (James 2:6) He's just shown them the picture of the man with the gold ring getting the seat of honor. Now he asks them to think about who the rich are to them.

The royal law is "Love your neighbor as yourself," friends. James says if they really fulfill it, "you are doing well." (James 2:8) It comes from Leviticus 19:18, and it fits this whole scene. Giving someone the standing spot isn't exactly loving them like yourself.

The answer is True, friends. James says, "But if you show favoritism, you sin and are convicted by the law as transgressors." (James 2:9) He doesn't call it a little social slip. He calls it sin, and he says it right after the royal law, so the comparison is hard to miss.

The answer is False, friends. James says, "Whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles at just one point is guilty of breaking all of it." (James 2:10) So one stumble isn't counted alone. He's showing that favoritism can't be shrugged off as a small thing.

The word is lawbreaker, friends. James says, "If you do not commit adultery, but do commit murder, you have become a lawbreaker." (James 2:11) Keeping one command doesn't cancel breaking another. It's the same One who gave both.

The answer is anyone who has not been merciful, friends. James says, "For judgment without mercy will be shown to anyone who has not been merciful." (James 2:13) Mercy is what the favoritism was missing. Handing out seats by gold rings isn't mercy.

The word is mercy, friends! James ends with, "Mercy triumphs over judgment." (James 2:13) After all that talk about law and sin, that last line is a good one to land on. It follows right after the line about those who haven't been merciful.
